claims.text: Increasing short-range order in refractory high-entropy alloys elevates the activation energy for dislocation movement.
A higher activation energy for dislocation movement leads to enhanced yield strength.
Increasing short-range order alters the thermoelastic behavior of refractory high-entropy alloys.
The proposed initial model is a single-phase BCC refractory HEA configured as a random solid solution with minimal SRO.
Hybrid Monte Carlo/molecular-dynamics simulations can systematically introduce and vary SRO in the alloy.
The comparison is to be performed at approximately 700–1200 °C while holding alloy composition, strain rate, and single-phase BCC structure constant.
SRO locally modifies the lattice environment.
Enhanced SRO increases local lattice distortions.
Local lattice fluctuations and distortions introduce energy barriers against dislocation motion in single-phase refractory HEAs.
SRO-induced barriers control dislocation nucleation and movement.
Greater SRO increases yield strength relative to a random solid solution.
Greater SRO produces measurable changes in thermoelastic properties such as elastic stiffness.
Rapid quenching generates a random-solid-solution baseline with minimal SRO.
The proposed SRO mechanism operates throughout 700–1200 °C in single-phase BCC refractory HEAs without major secondary phases or segregation.
The quantitative changes in activation energy and mechanical properties remain uncertain and simulation results may not directly extrapolate to experiments.
Comparing random and SRO-enriched models under identical temperature and strain-rate conditions is intended to isolate the effect of SRO.
Failure to observe statistically significant increases in dislocation activation energy and yield strength or a change in thermoelastic response would falsify the hypothesis.
